blocks.title: Multi-brand design tokens — Hero
blocks.intro: One set of __tokens__, every brand, every product
blocks.content: I designed and built the token pipeline that lets [N] product teams ship [N] brands from a single component library.

blocks.title: Multi-brand design tokens — Intro
blocks.overview: Each brand had forked the component library to change colours and type, so fixes landed [N] times or not at all. I replaced the forks with a tiered token system generated from Figma variables, and moved brands to theme files instead of code.

blocks.title: The problem
blocks.content: Brand changes meant forking components, and forks drifted within weeks.

blocks.title: Forks everywhere
blocks.body:
An audit of the [N] products found **[N] button variants** and [N] shades of the primary blue. Each brand team owned a fork of the library, so an accessibility fix had to be made, reviewed and released [N] times.

The cost showed up as:

- Slow rebrands: [N] weeks for a colour change
- Inconsistent accessibility: focus styles missing in [N] of [N] forks
- Design and code disagreeing about what "primary" meant

images.placeholder: Audit grid: every primary button variant found, on a neutral background
Colour audit: swatches of every 'primary blue' with hex values
Same screen in two forks, differences annotated

blocks.title: Architecture
blocks.content: Three token tiers: raw values, semantic roles, and component decisions.

blocks.title: Tiers, not themes
blocks.body:
Raw tokens hold values (`blue-600`). Semantic tokens name intent (`color-action-primary`). Component tokens decide where intent applies (`button-background`). Brands only override the semantic tier, so a brand is a file, not a fork.

I rejected per-component theming: it gave brands more control but brought the drift back.
